<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Alma S. Adams, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Summer L. Lee>: The leading voice in support of this legislation appears to be the NAR and its state affiliates. NAR's materials describe its efforts as ``protect[ing] independent contractors'' from federal employment and labor laws adopting a streamlined employment test (the ``ABC test'') in place of the FLSA economic realities test and the common law control test used in the National Labor Relations Act.\29\
\29\NAR Brief, supra note 9.
To the extent that the NAR has a rationale at all for this bill, it appears to be a rehash of an argument that the Majority has brought to this Committee in other contexts multiple times since the 118th Congress about supposedly radical changes to the FLSA employment test:
• Before the Trump Rule: The economic
realities test, discussed above, was the test for FLSA
going back to the 1940s.
• The Trump Rule: A Trump Administration rule,
published in January 2021 (Trump Rule), completely
rewrote this test.\30\ It emphasized two factors above
all--a worker's opportunity to make a profit under the
arrangement, and the worker's control over schedule or
other aspects of the job.\31\ If a worker could
arguably make a profit and had control over something
basic such as his or her own schedule, those facts
could alone be enough to overwhelm other factors of the
Trump Rule's new test. According to the Economic Policy
Institute (EPI), the Trump Rule would have cost workers
more than $3 billion yearly in lost wages.\32\ Courts
either questioned the validity of the Trump Rule\33\ or
waved it away as an interpretation of law that does not
trump authoritative court precedent.\34\
\30\Independent Contractor Status Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, 86 Fed. Reg. 1168 (Jan. 7, 2021).
\31\Id.
\32\Heidi Shierholz, EPI Comments on Independent Contractor Status Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, Econ. Pol'y Inst. (Oct. 26, 2020), https://www.epi.org/publication/epi-comments-on-independent-contractor-status-under-the-fair-labor-standards-act/.
\33\Wallen v. TendoNova Corp., No. 20-cv-790-SE, 2022 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21126, *9, 2022 WL 17128983 (D.N.H. Nov. 22, 2022).
\34\Harris v. Diamond Dolls of Nev., No. 3:19-cv-00598-RCJ CBC, 2022 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 166300, *4-*5, 2022 WL 4125474 (D. Nev. July 26, 2022).
• The Biden Rule: The Biden Administration
attempted to simply withdraw the Trump Rule but, after
that move was rejected by a federal district court in
Texas, opted to replace it in with a January 2024 rule
that restores the decades-old economic realities test
(Biden Rule).\35\ The Biden Rule clarifies that the
ultimate question of the economic realities test is
whether workers are running their own businesses
(making them truly independent contractors) or are
dependent on finding work in the business of
another.\36\ It also adds helpful explanations for how
and why each non-exhaustive factor in the economic
realities test helps answer this ultimate question.\37\
\35\Employee or Independent Contractor Classification Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, 89 Fed. Reg. 1638 (Jan. 10, 2024) [hereinafter Biden Rule].
\36\Id. at 1742 (revising 29 C.F.R. Sec. 795.105(a)).
\37\Id. at 1742-1743.
• Attacks on the Biden Rule: The Republicans
have repeatedly criticized the Biden Rule as though it
radically rewrites the law.\38\ Instead, it merely
restores the law as it was applied from 1938 to 2021.
The Republicans have also argued that the purpose of
the Biden Rule is not to fix the damage of the Trump
Rule but, instead, to attack independent contracting in
its entirety by adopting the AB 5 version of the ABC
Test. DOL reiterated more than once in the Biden Rule
that it lacks the power to adopt the ABC test and
merely restored the longstanding economic realities
test laid out by the courts decades ago.\39\ (On-demand
gig companies such as Uber and Instacart, which mounted
a $224 million campaign in California for a ballot
initiative carving themselves out of AB 5,\40\ agreed
with the Biden Administration on this point.\41\) Five
court challenges against the Biden Rule are still
pending. Three were dismissed on standing grounds; of
those, two are being appealed, and the third is likely
to be appealed soon. Two others are on appeal for other
reasons, with each delayed at the request of the Trump
Administration.\42\
\38\See, e.g., Empowering the Modern Worker: Hearing before the Subcomm. on Wrkf. Prots. of the H. Comm. on Educ. & Wrkf., 119th Cong.
(2025); Examining Biden's War on Independent Contractors: Hearing before the Subcomm. on Wrkf. Prots. of the H. Comm. on Educ. & the Wrkf., 118th Cong. (2023).
\39\DOL could not have stated it more plainly: ``[DOL] is not adopting an ABC test. [DOL] continues to believe that an ABC test would be inconsistent with Supreme Court and federal appellate precedent interpreting and applying the FLSA, and therefore, this final rule declines to adopt an ABC test.'' Biden Rule, supra note 35, at 1662 (emphases added).
\40\Brian Chen & Laura Padin, Prop 22 Was a Failure for California's App-Based Workers. Now, It's Also Unconstitutional., Nat'l Emp. L. Proj. (Sept. 16, 2021), https://www.nelp.org/blog/prop-22-unconstitutional/.
\41\``The Department of Labor rule released today does not reclassify any workers,'' said Instacart in a statement on the Biden Rule. ``It merely provides interpretation guidance on the factors the agency plans to consider when determining workers status under federal minimum wage law.'' Id.
\42\Rebecca Rainey & Chris Marr, Punching In: The Court Battles Awaiting DOL's New Leaders, Bloomberg (Mar. 17, 2025), https:// www.bgov.com/next/news/ST9FP5DWLU68.
• The Trump II Rollback: On May 1, 2025, the
Trump Administration issued a Field Assistance Bulletin
(FAB)--which provides guidance to DOL field staff on
how to enforce and interpret the law--declaring that
DOL ``will no longer apply the 2024 Rule's analysis
when determining employee versus independent contractor
status in FLSA investigations.''\43\ Instead, DOL is
relying on previous guidance issued under the Trump and
George W. Bush administrations, while it is considering
``whether to rescind the regulation.''\44\ Although the
2024 rule can still be relied upon in private
litigation while it remains in effect, this FAB signals
the Trump administration's likely plan to rescind the
2024 rule and enact another employee classification
test more in line with its own 2021 rule.
\43\Wage & Hr. Div., U.S. Dep't of Lab., Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-1, FLSA Independent Contractor Misclassification Enforcement Guidance (May 1, 2025), https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WHD/fab/ fab2025-1.pdf?lec6tn7bd.
\44\Id.
Despite their positions, the NAR and the Majority have yet to bring up any case in which FLSA has applied to real estate agents or direct sellers in the first instance. Moreover, even if FLSA applied in a specific arrangement, the outside sales exemption would still allow for traditional pay practices to apply. There is, simply, no evidence of any problem at all in these industries that requires an amendment of the nation's fundamental wage protection and child labor law. Threatening Independence
If real estate agents and direct sellers are categorically exempted from the FLSA employment definition, nothing would stop their respective upstream power players from denying the workers the independence that currently characterizes their work. A real estate broker could, for example, require set office hours and limit agents' flexibility in highly prescriptive ways, exercising the degree of control characteristic of employers under both the economic realities and common law control tests.
Leaving FLSA as it is, by contrast, protects the independence and flexibility that these workers currently enjoy, while accommodating the pay practices that define the industries. Putting Low-Wage Call Center Workers at Risk
A DOL investigation in the first Trump Administration led to a FLSA wage theft enforcement action against a call center business in Las Vegas. The Defendants argued that they were allowed to characterize their workers as independent contractors paid solely for their sales because of the tax code treatment of direct sellers. A federal court disagreed. The court held, first, that the tax law has no bearing on FLSA. The court also noted that the workers were not engaged in independent sales work but, instead, simply read predefined scripts and did not exercise skills or sales acumen in the course of their work. Moreover, the workers were not hired for their salesmanship but, instead, for their ability to read and sound acceptable in a telephone call. Accordingly, FLSA applied and protected these low-wage call center workers' rights to a minimum wage and premium payment for overtime hours.\45\
\45\Acosta v. Wellfleet Commc'ns, LLC, No. 2:16-cv-02353-GMN-GWF, 2018 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 168671 (D. Nev. Sept. 29, 2018).
In the world created by this bill, these workers would have been out of luck. These low-wage call center workers would have been categorically excluded from FLSA's coverage. As a result, they would have lost not only their case but also any right to a minimum wage, overtime pay, equal pay on the basis of sex, privacy for expressing breast milk, and protected family and medical leave.
Conclusion
For the reasons stated above, Committee Democrats unanimously opposed H.R. 3495 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on September 17, 2025. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Alma S. Adams,
Mark DeSaulnier,
Jahana Hayes,
Summer L. Lee,
Members of Congress.
